I am going to talk about this game released for the PlayStation 2. Romancing Saga.

It reminds me of SaGa Frontier which was released for Playstation 1. These 2 games have very similar features and I was able to adapt to the play style well. Romancing SaGa has a much more fleshed out playstyle/story progression for each character. It felt like a true successor to the SaGa Frontier Classic playstyle/story telling. Sadly SaGa Frontier had budget problems which cut the game production short. Of course SaGa Frontier already had a large amount of content and a the character storylines had and ending which connected in your game save file once you beat the storyline with each character. Once all finished you have access to a hub room. To enter this hub room the last storyline you finished the game with after** finishing all storylines will enter this hub and have access to every final boss in the game and other nifty things to play with.

I have yet to do that with Romancing SaGa as I'm still only on one storyline. Albert. I will write a review once I'm finished, but as of right now. I'm really enjoying the game and Its something strange thinking about such concepts in a game will never be made again. Like an old book. At least this classic is still new for me...

Ingredients

  • 6 egg yolks
  • 1/3 cup sugar
  • 3/4 cup Marsala wine (any sweet dessert wine works)
  • 1 teaspoon grated lemon peel
  • Ground cinnamon
  • Vanilla extract
  • Strawberries, raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, etc (for covering - most fruits will do)

DIRECTIONS

  • Place egg yolks and sugar in a large, round-bottomed bowl. Add grated lemon peel and a pinch of cinnamon and a drop of vanilla extract (though in my kitchen, this turns into more than a small drop) to the yolk mixture. Pour in the wine.
  • Half-fill a pot with water, bring the water to a simmer and reduce the heat to low. Set the bowl containing the custard mixture over the water; the bottom of the bowl should not touch the water. Whisk the custard mixture, making sure that the water does not boil. This ensures that a gentle, even heat thickens the mixture without curdling it. Whisking traps air in the yolks for a light, fluffy mixture. Whisking too quickly, such as with a mixer, will cause things to congeal and become unappealing (learned from sad sad experience).
  • Continue whisking for about 10 minutes (probably a bit longer, like 5 more mins), until the mixture triples in volume, froths up and becomes pale. When it reaches the desired consistency, take the container of custard out of the pot. Slightly thickened, the custard can be used as a sauce. Longer cooking will thicken the custard further, giving it the texture of mousse. Continue whisking for a minute or two to prevent the custard from sticking to its container.
  • If you made this too early, feel free to cover the fruit with it and pop it in the fridge. It stays tasty this way, and doesn't flatten too hard. Cooling it over the fruit also allows it to marinate, and the fruits become more infused with the sweet wine flavor.

Enjoy!
